newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel bankers said to reach debt deal.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel bankers said to reach debt deal.

text.p: The steering committee of bankers to Eurotunnel have agreed final terms for restructuring the Channel Tunnel operator's nine billion pounds ($14.6 billion) of debt, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday.
Eurotunnel announced on Monday it would be reporting its results for 1996 on April 24.

The paper said the final version of the restructuring plan, which still has to be approved by Eurotunnel's shareholders and all 225 banks in the lending syndicate, had been modified "only marginally" from the plan initialled by the company and its bankers last October.

But the agreement was subject to two conditions, namely that last November's fire did not alter Eurotunnel's traffic and cashflow predictions and also that it did not cause radical changes in how freight vehicles were carried through the tunnel, the Financial Times said.
Freight vehicle services have been suspended since the fire, while the authorities decide whether the design of the open-sided wagons which take lorries through the tunnel are safe.
Eurotunnel announced on April 4 it did not believe a costly redesign would be necessary but the final decision lies with the Safety Authority.
The steering committee's 20 instructing banks should now approve the deal later this month, opening the way for a special shareholders' meeting to vote on the deal in July, the newspaper said.
It would then be up to the full syndicate of lenders to approve the plan before the end of the year.

The Financial Times said the banks' steering committee was believed to have discussed several tactics to win over all the lenders to the restructuring deal, including the idea of launching a formal secondary market in Eurotunnel debt.

"A number of banks have already sold on Eurotunnel loans on the unofficial grey market, but a secondary market would allow them to fully cede their obligations, including all voting rights," the paper said.

"The efforts to buy up a relatively small proportion of the total value of the loans outstanding to Eurotunnel could help persuade a number of the more reluctant banks to agree to the restructuring," it said.
